questions.question_text: A Vermont tenant signs a 10-month lease at $1,200 per month. Under state law, what is the maximum security deposit the landlord may collect?
questions.correct_answer: There is no statewide cap on the amount
distractors: $600, equal to half of one month's rent
questions.explanation: Vermont's security deposit law, 9 V.S.A. § 4461, sets no statewide limit on the amount a landlord may collect. It governs how deposits are held and returned, not their size. A few municipalities such as Burlington cap deposits at one month's rent by local ordinance, but there is no statewide maximum.

questions.question_text: A Vermont tenant with an 18-month lease at $900 per month is asked for a $2,000 security deposit. Under state law, is this amount lawful?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, Vermont sets no statewide deposit cap
distractors: Only if the tenant agrees in writing
questions.explanation: Vermont law (9 V.S.A. § 4461) does not cap the size of a security deposit, so a $2,000 deposit is lawful under state law. The statute regulates how deposits are held and returned, not the amount collected. A few municipalities limit deposits by local ordinance, but no statewide maximum applies.

questions.question_text: Within how many days must a Vermont landlord return a security deposit after the tenant vacates?
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4461 requires the landlord to return the deposit with an itemized statement of any deductions within 14 days of the date the landlord discovers the tenant has vacated (60 days for seasonal rentals not intended as a primary residence). Missing the deadline forfeits the right to withhold anything.

questions.question_text: A Vermont landlord willfully fails to return a tenant's $1,000 security deposit within the required timeframe. What penalty may the court impose?
questions.correct_answer: Double the amount plus attorney fees
distractors: Return of only the deposit amount
Triple damages plus all court costs
A $500 civil fine per day of delay
questions.explanation: Willful failure to return a security deposit within 14 days in Vermont can result in the landlord paying double the deposit amount plus the tenant's attorney fees.

questions.question_text: A Vermont landlord deducts $300 from a security deposit for normal carpet wear after 3 years of tenancy. Is this deduction lawful?
questions.correct_answer: No, normal wear and tear cannot be deducted
distractors: Yes, carpet costs are always deductible
Yes, if properly documented with photographs
Yes, for any tenancy exceeding 2 years
questions.explanation: Under 9 V.S.A. § 4461 a landlord may retain deposit funds only for nonpayment of rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear (and not caused by events outside the tenant's control), unpaid utilities or other charges the tenant agreed to pay, and the cost of removing property the tenant abandoned. Ordinary carpet wear over three years is none of those.

questions.question_text: A Vermont tenant fails to pay rent. How many days does the landlord's pay-or-quit notice give the tenant?
questions.explanation: For nonpayment of rent in Vermont, the landlord must provide a 14-day notice to pay or quit. This gives the tenant two weeks to either pay the overdue rent or vacate the premises.

questions.question_text: A Vermont tenant violates a lease provision by keeping an unauthorized pet. What notice period must the landlord provide?
questions.explanation: For lease violations other than nonpayment, Vermont requires a 30-day notice to cure or quit. The tenant has 30 days to correct the violation or vacate the property.

questions.question_text: A Vermont month-to-month tenant with no written rental agreement has lived in the unit 3 years. How much no-cause notice must the landlord give?
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4467(c): where there is no written rental agreement, no-cause termination requires at least 60 days' notice if the tenant has continuously occupied the premises two years or less, and at least 90 days' notice if more than two years. The shorter 30/60-day periods in § 4467(b) apply to tenancies under a WRITTEN rental agreement, measured before the end of the stated term.

questions.question_text: A Vermont tenant engages in serious criminal activity on the premises. What is the minimum notice period for eviction?
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4467(b)(2) allows a 14-day notice where the tenant's breach involves criminal activity, activity that threatens the health or safety of other residents, or illegal drug activity — shorter than the 30-day notice for an ordinary lease breach, but still a notice period.

questions.question_text: A Vermont month-to-month tenant with no written rental agreement has rented for 18 months. What no-cause notice is required?
questions.explanation: Under 9 V.S.A. § 4467(c), a no-cause termination of a month-to-month tenancy with no written rental agreement requires at least 60 days' notice when the tenant has occupied the premises for two years or less, and 90 days when longer. Eighteen months falls in the 60-day band. (A weekly tenancy takes 21 days' notice.)

questions.question_text: A Vermont apartment's furnace fails in January and the landlord ignores repair requests for two weeks. Which tenant remedy fits?
distractors: Repair and deduct the full cost of a new furnace
Terminate the lease with no notice and stop paying
File a criminal complaint against the landlord
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4458 lets a tenant withhold rent for the period of noncompliance once the landlord has actual notice, has failed to repair within a reasonable time, and the defect materially affects health and safety — a failed furnace in January qualifies. Repair-and-deduct under § 4459 is narrower: it applies only to a MINOR defect, only after 30 days from notice, and is capped at one-half of one month's rent.

questions.question_text: A Vermont tenant reports a building code violation to the health department. The landlord then serves a termination notice. What legal protection applies?
distractors: The landlord may proceed if cause exists
The tenant must prove malice in court
No protection exists for this scenario
questions.explanation: Vermont prohibits retaliatory eviction. A landlord cannot terminate a tenancy in retaliation for a tenant exercising legal rights such as reporting code violations or requesting repairs.

questions.question_text: Under Vermont law, when must a residential lease be in writing to be enforceable?
questions.correct_answer: When the term is longer than one year
distractors: Always — Vermont requires every tenancy to be in writing
Only for tenancies of six months or longer
Only for tenancies of two years or longer
questions.explanation: Vermont's Residential Rental Agreements Act (9 V.S.A. ch. 137) does not require a written lease — a tenant is a legal tenant with or without one. The writing requirement comes from the statute of frauds, which covers a lease of land for a term longer than one year. Note the same one-year line in 27 V.S.A. § 342, which requires leases longer than one year to be acknowledged and recorded to bind third parties.

questions.question_text: A Vermont landlord wants to raise the rent on a month-to-month tenancy. What does 9 V.S.A. § 4455 require?
questions.correct_answer: At least 60 days' actual notice before the increase takes effect
distractors: Nothing — rent may be changed at any time
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4455 provides that an increase in rent takes effect on the first day of the rental period following no less than 60 days' actual notice to the tenant. Vermont sets no statutory list of terms a written lease must contain, but § 4454 voids any provision that attempts to circumvent the obligations and remedies of chapter 137.

questions.question_text: A Vermont landlord's rental unit has persistent mold from a leaking roof. The tenant withholds rent until repairs are made. Is this lawful?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, rent withholding is a valid remedy
distractors: No, tenants must always pay rent
Yes, but only after 90 days' notice
questions.explanation: 9 V.S.A. § 4458 permits a tenant to withhold rent for the period of the landlord's noncompliance where the landlord had actual notice, failed to repair within a reasonable time, and the condition materially affects health and safety. Persistent mold from a leaking roof breaches the landlord's habitability obligation under § 4457.
